concepts.label: Production of Sound by Vibrations
concepts.cardText: In Activity 10.1 a rubber band stretched across an open box produces sound when plucked, as long as it is stretched and vibrating; once the vibration stops, so does the sound. So sound is produced by vibrations. Vibration refers to the periodic to and fro motion (oscillations) of an object. Sound can be produced by vibrating strings, membranes, air columns and many other vibrating objects, and the object that produces sound is called the source of the sound. In humans and some other animals sound is produced by the vibration of vocal cords, tightly stretched muscular flaps inside the voice box or larynx in the throat. Grasshoppers and crickets rub their wings or legs to produce sound. A tuning fork is a U-shaped metal bar with a stem, whose prongs are struck on a rubber pad to make them vibrate; a vibrating prong touching water makes waves on the surface, indicating that the prongs are vibrating.

concepts.label: Sound Needs a Medium to Propagate
concepts.cardText: Sound can also travel through solids: with an ear against a desk you can hear a knock on it. It also travels through liquids: tapped spoons submerged in water can still be heard. Sound can travel or propagate through solids, liquids and gases. The material through which sound propagates is called a medium, and a space where there is no medium (matter) is referred to as vacuum. In the vacuum bell jar experiment an electric bell is kept in a bell jar and as air is sucked out the sound becomes fainter; once a near vacuum is reached almost no sound can be heard even though the bell can be seen ringing, and when air is let back in the sound can be heard again and gradually becomes as loud as before. This experiment shows that sound cannot propagate in vacuum: sound needs a medium, which can be a solid, a liquid or a gas. In outer space, which is a near vacuum, sound cannot propagate, so astronauts doing spacewalks cannot directly hear each other speak or hear metal objects clanking, and communicate through special devices fitted into their spacesuits.

concepts.label: Compressions, Rarefactions and the Sound Wave
concepts.cardText: In the slinky activity a push and pull at one end creates regions where the turns are closer together than usual and other regions where they are more spread out, and these regions travel along the slinky, but a mark on a turn does not travel; it only oscillates about its position of rest parallel to the direction of the disturbance. Sound moves similarly through a medium, the closeness or spreading out of the turns representing the higher or lower density of air. In a tube with an oscillating piston, a forward motion pushes nearby air particles and compresses the air in a small region, increasing its density: this region of higher density is a compression (C). A backward motion makes the air in that region less dense: a region of lower density is a rarefaction (R). As the piston oscillates, compressions and rarefactions are produced alternately and travel away from the source. The disturbance consisting of a series of alternating compressions and rarefactions propagating through a medium, without the actual flow of the particles of the medium, is called a sound wave, and the direction in which it travels is the direction of propagation. The particles of the medium do not travel with the wave; they just vibrate about their mean positions.

concepts.label: Longitudinal and Mechanical Waves
concepts.cardText: In sound waves the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of propagation of the disturbance. Waves in which the particles vibrate in a direction parallel to the direction of wave propagation are known as longitudinal waves. Without a material medium sound waves cannot propagate; waves that require a material medium for propagation are called mechanical waves, and sound is a type of mechanical wave. Mechanical waves are of two types, longitudinal and transverse; in a transverse wave the particles vibrate in a direction perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. Not all waves need a medium: light, which is a transverse wave, can travel through vacuum, which is why light from the Sun and other stars can reach the Earth. A small source producing sound in all directions causes compressions and rarefactions that spread through the surrounding medium as spherical waves. Sudden loud sounds such as thunder arise when air or gases heated rapidly expand very rapidly, creating a sudden disturbance in the air density that travels outward.

concepts.label: Sound Carries Energy
concepts.cardText: In Activity 10.6 grains sprinkled on a stretched sheet jump when a loud sound is produced near it, though the source does not touch the sheet: the sound propagating through air reaches the sheet and makes it vibrate, and this vibration causes the grains to move. This shows that sound is a form of energy. When the source of sound vibrates it transfers energy to the surrounding medium, and as sound waves propagate the vibration of particles of the medium and their collisions with other particles result in the transfer of energy. In the propagation of a sound wave it is the energy that is transferred, not the particles of the medium. A microphone converts sound energy to electrical energy: sound waves make a thin membrane called a diaphragm vibrate and the vibrations are converted into an electrical signal. A speaker does the opposite: an electrical signal makes a cone or diaphragm vibrate, which produces sound.

concepts.label: Graphical Representation of a Sound Wave
concepts.cardText: As a sound wave propagates, at any given instant of time the density of the medium varies periodically with distance from the source. When this is graphed, the distance is plotted on the x-axis and the density of the medium on the y-axis, with the average density marked as a horizontal dashed line, and the density varies above and below it. In the region of a compression the density increases above the average density and the highest point represents the maximum density; thereafter the density decreases and falls below the average density in the region of rarefaction, with the lowest point representing the minimum density. The highest point is called the crest and the lowest point is called the trough of the wave. Another way to represent a sound wave is to plot the variation of density of the medium with time at a particular location.

concepts.label: Wavelength, Frequency and Time Period
concepts.cardText: The distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs is called the wavelength of a wave, usually represented by the Greek letter lambda, with SI unit the metre. The change in the density of the medium at a fixed point from maximum to minimum and then again to maximum makes one complete oscillation. The number of density oscillations at a fixed point per unit time is the frequency of the sound wave, with SI unit per second, also called the hertz (Hz). The time taken for one complete density oscillation at a fixed point is the time period, represented by T, with SI unit second. The time period and frequency are inversely related; a shorter time period corresponds to a higher frequency. Everyday sounds contain a mixture of many frequencies, while nearly single frequency sounds can be made by striking a tuning fork or by oral whistling. Each musical note has a distinct frequency: in the Sa, Re, Ga activity the frequency is lowest for Sa and gradually increases for the other notes.

concepts.label: Amplitude and Intensity
concepts.cardText: The amplitude of a sound wave is the maximum change in the density of air in a compression (or a rarefaction) compared to the average density; a larger change in density corresponds to a larger amplitude. The amplitude and the amount of energy a wave carries are related: a wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy than one with a smaller amplitude, as seen when the plate is struck harder and the grains jump higher. The amount of sound energy passing through a unit area perpendicular to the direction of propagation in a unit time is called the intensity of sound. As the sound wave travels away from the source it spreads over a larger area, and since the energy must be conserved, the same energy is spread over a larger area, so the intensity decreases with distance from the source. Sounds produced with initial larger amplitude carry more energy and can travel a larger distance before the intensity reduces to zero.

concepts.label: Speed of Sound
concepts.cardText: The speed of sound describes how fast sound waves propagate through a medium, that is how fast the density disturbances propagate. It can be defined as the distance which a point on a wave, such as a crest or a trough, travels in unit time. In one time period the disturbance covers one wavelength, so speed equals wavelength multiplied by frequency. The speed of sound depends on the medium through which it travels: it travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases; sound travels about 4 to 5 times faster in water and typically 15 to 20 times faster in solids than in air. In air, the speed also depends on temperature and humidity, and increases as they increase. In most media the speed depends only on the medium and not on the source or frequency: if the frequency of the source changes, the wavelength changes while the speed remains constant. Lightning is seen before thunder is heard because sound travels much slower than light.

concepts.label: Pitch and the Audible Range
concepts.cardText: The physical properties of sound, such as time period, wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed, are well-defined and can be measured, but how we experience sound is subjective, described by terms such as loudness and pitch which do not have simple relations with the physical properties. How frequency is perceived by humans is called pitch. Sounds perceived to be shrill, such as a whistle or a siren, have high pitch, while deep sounds like thunder or an aircraft rumble have low pitch. In general high pitch sounds have higher frequency and low pitch sounds lower frequency, although the exact relation is complicated. The audible range of human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), varying from person to person and decreasing with age. Sound waves with frequency below 20 Hz are called infrasonic waves, and those above 20 kHz are called ultrasonic waves. Humans cannot hear infrasound or ultrasound but some animals can: dogs, cats, bats and dolphins can detect ultrasound, while elephants can detect infrasound.

concepts.label: Loudness, Noise and Hearing
concepts.cardText: Humans perceive the amplitude of a sound wave as loudness. Sounds with larger amplitude are heard louder, while those with smaller amplitude sound softer, and the loudness decreases as we move farther from the source. In everyday language loudness and intensity are used interchangeably, but intensity is a measurable quantity whereas loudness depends on the listener's hearing ability. Loudness is commonly measured in decibels (dB): very soft sounds like rustling leaves are a few dB, normal conversation is about 60 dB, and very loud sounds such as firecrackers can exceed 100 dB, and even a small increase in the dB level means a large increase in sound intensity. Unwanted or harmful sound is called noise, and noise pollution is a severe problem; exposure above recommended limits, especially for long durations, can affect health, sleep and hearing, and prolonged exposure to loud sound can lead to hearing loss, which can be tested using audiograms. People with hearing loss may use hearing aids, which consist of a microphone, amplifier and speaker.

concepts.label: Tone, Musical Note, Timbre and Octave
concepts.cardText: A tone is a sound of a single frequency, like that produced by a tuning fork or by oral whistling. A musical note, like the sound produced by plucking a tanpura string or singing, is a combination of a lowest frequency called the fundamental and higher frequencies called overtones, which together create a rich and pleasant sound. Even when different instruments such as a flute, ektara or tabla play the same note at the same loudness, each sounds unique; this quality is called timbre, and it comes from the shape, material and construction of the instrument, which determine the pattern and intensity of the overtones. An octave is the interval between two notes where one has double the frequency of the other, for example 200 Hz and 400 Hz, measured between their fundamental frequencies.

concepts.label: Reflection of Sound and Echo
concepts.cardText: Sound waves can bounce off obstacles like solids or liquids, which is known as the reflection of sound, and sound follows the same laws of reflection as light: the directions in which the sound is incident and reflected make equal angles with the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence, with all three in the same plane. One of the most common examples is an echo: if we shout near a mountain, a cliff or in a long corridor we may hear our voice again after some time because the sound reflects off the hard surface of a distant object and comes back to us. If the time gap between two sounds reaching us is at least 0.1 s we hear them as separate sounds; if it is less than 0.1 s we cannot clearly distinguish them, which is why echoes are not heard in a small room. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m per second, sound travels 34 m in 0.1 s, and since this covers the distance to the surface and back, the minimum distance for an echo is half of this, or 17 m. Echoes are stronger from hard, smooth surfaces; soft surfaces like curtains absorb sound and rough surfaces scatter it, so echoes are not heard clearly.

If it is less than 0.1 s, then we cannot clearly distinguish between them.
Note that 34 m would be the distance travelled by sound from the source to the reflecting surface and back.
Hence, the minimum echo distance is half of this or 17 m.
Echoes are stronger from hard and smooth surfaces that reflect sound.
Soft surfaces like curtains tend to absorb sound, while rough surfaces scatter it in different directions, and in such cases it is not possible to hear the echoes clearly.
In a room, the reflected sound reaches the ear 0.05 s after its production.

concepts.label: Reverberation
concepts.cardText: Sometimes emitted sound undergoes multiple reflections from the walls in a large hall or auditorium. Multiple reflections make sound persist after the source stops emitting sound, a phenomenon called reverberation. It occurs when sound reflections from surfaces arrive with a time difference less than 0.05 s. Modern auditoriums and large concert halls are architecturally designed to have desirable reverberations, which allow the audience everywhere to hear speech, music and other sounds clearly without distortions. Sound absorbing panels, upholstered chairs, curtains and other soft, porous surfaces reduce reverberations from unwanted sources, which otherwise could lead to a garbled sound. The Whispering Gallery of the Gol Gumbaz in Bijapur has a design that allows even a faint whisper to be heard multiple times across the large dome.

topics.title: Ultrasonic and infrasonic waves and their applications

concepts.label: Applications of Ultrasonic and Infrasonic Waves
concepts.cardText: Sound waves with frequencies outside the human audible range have important applications in science, medicine and technology. Infrasonic waves (less than 20 Hz) are used for detecting natural events such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, and for detecting severe storms since such waves travel long distances through air and the Earth. Ultrasonic waves (more than 20 kHz) are used for imaging internal organs without surgery, known as ultrasonography; for breaking kidney stones into smaller pieces which can then be passed out of the body; for ultrasonic welding and for cleaning delicate machine parts in industries; for detecting defects inside metal blocks during construction and industrial testing; and for locating objects when sound waves get reflected off them.

concepts.label: Echolocation and Sonar
concepts.cardText: Bats are nocturnal creatures that fly and search for prey in the dark without colliding with objects. Most bats emit short bursts of ultrasonic waves which are reflected from nearby objects, and by sensing the echoes the bat can determine the position of obstacles and prey. This ability to locate objects using reflected sound waves is called echolocation. Besides bats, dolphins, whales and some birds also use echolocation for navigation and hunting. Humans have adapted the same principle in underwater exploration through sonar (sound navigation and ranging): ultrasonic waves are sent into water and the reflected waves are analysed to determine the distance, direction and speed of underwater objects such as submarines or shipwrecks. For the distance, only half the time between sending and receiving the signal is used, because it travels to the object and back. Drones and aircraft produce characteristic low frequency sounds that sensitive sound sensors can detect, a method called audio surveillance.
